question_text:
The MCU below has a GPIO pin that can source up to 20 mA. You want to drive an LED (Vf = 2V) that needs at least 1 mA to light up. Vcc = 3.3V.

What is the minimum circuit between the GPIO pin and the LED?
answer_text:
A current-limiting resistor in series. Wire GPIO → R → LED → GND.

▶ Detailed Explanation

When the GPIO goes HIGH it acts as a 3.3V source. Apply KVL:

Vcc = V_R + Vf → V_R = 3.3V − 2V = 1.3V

Pick a target current — 10 mA is a comfortable brightness well under the 20 mA pin limit:

R = V_R / I = 1.3V / 10 mA = 130 Ω → nearest standard value: 150 Ω (gives ≈ 9 mA)

Going lower (e.g. 68 Ω → 19 mA) is fine too, as long as you stay under 20 mA. Going higher dims the LED.

Why not connect the LED directly? Without a resistor the LED's forward voltage alone sets the operating point. A tiny voltage overshoot drives exponentially more current — the LED burns out and the GPIO pin is damaged.
bonus_question_text: The LED is on but you want to control its brightness in software. How?
bonus_answer_text:
PWM — Pulse-Width Modulation.

Toggle the GPIO HIGH/LOW at a fixed frequency (e.g. 1 kHz). Your eyes low-pass-filter the flicker and perceive an average brightness proportional to the duty cycle (fraction of time the signal is HIGH).

  • 50% duty cycle → LED appears at half brightness
  • 10% duty cycle → LED appears at ~10% brightness
  • 100% duty cycle → full brightness (same as DC HIGH)

Most MCUs have dedicated PWM hardware peripherals so the CPU doesn't have to bit-bang the pin. The resistor value stays the same — PWM controls time, not peak current.
